summary: Defines Negative Trust Anchors, which let an operator turn off DNSSEC validation for specific domains. They are used to work around validation failures caused by a domain's own signing mistakes, so users can still reach it.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7646 describes a way for a resolver operator to keep serving a domain that has broken its own DNSSEC signing. The resolver is told to stop checking the signatures for that one domain and to behave as if it were never signed, while every other domain is still checked. The document is mostly about the care that has to be taken, because turning validation off can hide an attack as easily as it hides a mistake.

subtitle: A temporary way to stop validating one broken domain, so that a mistake in signing does not take a site offline.

tldr.problem: When a domain owner gets DNSSEC signing wrong, a validating resolver refuses to answer, and the users of that domain cannot reach it at all. The domain owner may not know, and the users usually blame their provider.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7646 defines a negative trust anchor: a local setting on a validating resolver that tells it to stop validating the chain for one domain and treat it as unsigned, while everything else stays validated.
tldr.outcome: The document sets tight rules on how such a setting may be used: only for a limited time, never automatically, never for more than one branch of the name tree, and only after a person has checked that the fault is a mistake rather than an attack. It also explains how to find out which it is.

today: RFC 7646 is an Informational RFC published in September 2015, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It describes a mechanism that resolvers implement under their own names, and it points at other documents for the operational practices it expects domain administrators to follow.

sections.title: Why a Negative Trust Anchor Exists
sections.content:
DNSSEC has entered widespread deployment, but the signing tools and the processes around signing are less mature and reliable than those for ordinary DNS administration. Operators of recursive resolvers, such as internet service providers, occasionally see domains managing their DNSSEC resource records incorrectly. That mismanagement causes validation failures, and then large numbers of end users cannot reach the domain at all. Users tend to read this as a failure of their provider or resolver operator, and some of them move to a resolver that does not validate, or complain to their provider, instead of seeing it as a failure of the domain they wanted to reach. Without a technique for this, that pressure may lead resolver operators to turn validation off, or never to deploy it.

The document defines negative trust anchors, which can be used during the transition to ubiquitous DNSSEC deployment. They are configured locally on a validating recursive resolver, to shield end users from DNSSEC-related errors by the authoritative name servers. They are meant to be temporary, implemented only by the organisation that needs one, and not passed on to anyone outside its administrative boundary. They concern DNSSEC only, and not public key infrastructures such as X.509.

Using one to disable validation temporarily for a specific misconfigured domain immediately restores access for end users. The domain's administrators can then fix their mistake, while the organisation that configured the anchor keeps validation switched on everywhere else and can still reach the broken domain.

There are three motivations. The first is to mitigate validation failures caused by misconfiguration: a domain can fail validation because of a genuine security problem or because the zone administrator made a mistake, and as domains move to DNSSEC the second is the more common cause, so administrators should read the operational practices document in full and pay particular attention to its section on key rollovers, which appear to cause many recent failures. Some failures also come from different software interpreting the standards differently, so a domain that is signed correctly may validate on one vendor's resolvers and fail on another's. The second motivation is the end-user experience: users neither know nor care about the resolution process, so a failure makes them suspect their provider is blocking the domain or that the provider's servers are slow, and they complain, which costs the provider money and may lead to public criticism. Using a negative trust anchor lets the provider fix access to that one domain without weakening security anywhere else. The third motivation is to stop users switching to a resolver that does not validate. A domain that fails validation may be under the control of an attacker, so switching to a non-validating resolver is not a recommended practice, is bad advice to give others, and is potentially harmful to the user's security.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing a domain correctly is harder than it should be, and when it goes wrong a validating resolver stops answering for it. The people affected cannot tell the difference between their provider misbehaving and the domain being broken, and some of them walk away from validation altogether. A negative trust anchor is a way for the provider to keep one broken domain working while everything else stays checked, so that providers are not pushed into turning validation off altogether.

sections.title: What a Negative Trust Anchor Is
sections.content:
Trust anchors are defined in RFC 5914. A trust anchor is what a validating caching resolver uses as a starting point for building the authentication chain for a signed DNS response. A negative trust anchor stops the validation of that authentication chain. Instead, the validator treats any upstream responses as if the zone were unsigned, and does not set the Authentic Data bit in the responses it sends to clients. It is worth being precise about what this is: it is a behaviour, and not a separate resource record.

A negative trust anchor can potentially be implemented at any level within the chain of trust, and it stops validation from that point in the chain downwards. Validation starts again if there is a positive trust anchor further down the chain. So if there is a negative trust anchor at example.com and a positive trust anchor at foo.bar.example.com, validation resumes for foo.bar.example.com and for anything below it.
sections.plainLanguage: A normal trust anchor is the point where the resolver starts checking signatures. A negative trust anchor is the opposite: it marks a point where the checking stops, and the resolver treats everything below it as unsigned. It can be put anywhere in the chain, and if a normal anchor appears further down, checking starts again from there.

sections.title: When and How to Use One
sections.content:
Technical personnel trained in the operation of DNS servers must confirm that a validation failure is due to misconfiguration, since a similar breakage could have occurred if an attacker gained access to a domain's authoritative servers and modified those records, or had the domain pointed at rogue authoritative servers. They should also confirm that the domain is not intentionally broken, and they should make a reasonable attempt to contact the domain owner, preferably before implementing the anchor. Involving trained technical personnel is costly, but operational experience suggests this is a very rare event, usually on the order of once per quarter or even less.

It is important for the resolver operator to confirm that the domain is still under the ownership and control of the legitimate owner, so that disabling validation for it does not direct users to an address under an attacker's control. Contacting the domain owner and telling them which DNSSEC records the operator is seeing allows the operator to tell a misconfiguration from an attack. Where the failure affects a top-level domain or a popular name, such as one of the top hundred sites, content or services could be inaccessible for a great many users, and it may be appropriate to use an anchor as soon as the misconfiguration is confirmed.

Once a domain has been confirmed to fail validation because of a DNSSEC misconfiguration, the operator may choose to use an anchor for that domain or sub-domain. This tells the recursive resolver to temporarily not perform DNSSEC validation at or in the misconfigured domain, which immediately restores access for end users while the administrator corrects the mistake. It does not, and should not, involve turning validation off more broadly.

The rules on applicability are strict. An anchor must only be used for a limited duration, and implementations should let the operator set an end time and date for it, preferably in the resolver's configuration, though in the short term other systems or processes may achieve this. Use of an anchor must not be automatic. It should be used only for a specific domain or sub-domain and must not affect validation of other names up the authentication chain: an anchor for zone1.example.com would affect only names at or below it, and validation would still be performed on example.com, on .com and on the root. It should also not affect names in another branch of the tree, such as example.net. An anchor for example.com would affect only names within example.com, with validation still performed on .com and the root, and in that scenario, if there is a manually configured trust anchor for zone1.example.com, validation would be performed for that name and its subdomains.
sections.plainLanguage: Nobody should install one of these on a hunch. A trained person has to check that the fault really is the domain's own mistake and not an attack, and that the domain still belongs to who it did, and the operator should try to contact the owner first. The setting must have an end date, must never be applied automatically, and must not spill over to other names: an anchor on one branch of the name tree leaves the rest of the tree fully validated.

sections.title: Managing and Removing Them
sections.content:
While negative trust anchors have proved useful in the early stages of DNSSEC adoption, domain owners are ultimately responsible for managing their DNS records and ensuring they are configured correctly. Most current implementations of validating resolvers follow RFC 4033 in configuring a trust anchor, using either a public key in a DNSKEY record or a hash of a public key in a DS record. Different validators use different configuration names for an anchor.

An anchor placed at a node where there is a configured positive trust anchor must take precedence over that trust anchor, effectively disabling it, and implementations may issue a warning or an informational message so that operators are not surprised.

End users may wonder why a domain that fails validation still resolves with a supposedly validating resolver, so implementors should consider disclosing the anchors that are in place or were in place in the past, for example on a website. This matters because there is currently no special DNS response code that could tell end users or applications that an anchor is in place. Such disclosures should ideally include both the data and the time the anchor was put in place and when it was removed.

Removal is where the care is needed, because using an anchor once the zone validates correctly again can have security consequences. Implementors should periodically attempt to validate the domain while the anchor is in place, until validation succeeds again. Anchors must expire automatically when their configured lifetime ends, and the lifetime should not exceed a week. There is limited experience with what this value should be, but at least one large vendor has documented customer feedback suggesting that a week is reasonable, based on expectations of how long failures take to fix or to be forgotten, and operational experience may refine this further. Before removing an anchor, all the authoritative resolvers listed in the zone should be checked, though because of anycast and load balancers it may not be possible to check every instance.

Once testing succeeds, the anchor should be removed as soon as is reasonably possible. One possible way to decide automatically is to send a periodic query for the Start of Authority record type at the anchor's node; if the answer is one that can be validated, whether that is the record itself or a NOERROR with no data and the right denial records, the anchor is presumed no longer necessary and is removed. Implementations should do this by default, but it is not always right: if www.example.com has a bad signature while the SOA record for example.com is fine, the check would remove the anchor too early, so implementations may let the operator override it. When the anchor is removed, the implementation should remove all cached entries at and below its node.
sections.plainLanguage: Anchors have to end. The resolver should keep trying to validate the domain while the anchor is in place, and the anchor must expire by itself at a fixed time, no more than a week after it was set. Before it is removed, every authoritative server for the domain should be checked, and when it is removed the cached answers below it should be thrown away.

sections.title: Telling Misconfiguration From Attack
sections.content:
Discovering that a domain is broken by an operator error rather than by an attack is not trivial, and the examples given should be vetted by an experienced professional before anyone decides to install an anchor. One of the key things to look for is consistency and history, so it helps to be able to look at the server's DNS traffic over a long period, or to have a database of DNS names and the answers given for them, often called a passive DNS database. DNSViz also stores DNSSEC-related data historically, but the drawback is that it has to have tested the domain before the incident occurs.

The first and easiest check is whether the failure is consistent across different software implementations. If it is not, the vendor where it fails should be told, so that they can look more deeply into the issue. The next step is to work out the actual failure mode, for which several tools are available, including DNSViz, the Verisign DNSSEC debugger and Zonemaster. Most are open source and can be installed locally, but using them over the internet has the advantage of giving a view from a different point.

Once the error is understood, it has to be checked for consistency around the world and from all the authoritative servers, using dig or DNS looking glasses. An error that is consistently the same is more likely to have been caused by an operator than by an attack. If the output from the authoritative server is consistently different from the output of the resolvers, that hints at an attack rather than an error, unless the client subnet extension is being applied to the domain. The last check is to look at the actual DNS data: is the result of the query still the same, or has it changed? A great many DNSSEC errors occur at moments when the DNSSEC data changes while the record someone wants to reach stays the same, so unchanged data is an indication, though not a guarantee, that the error was caused by the operator. The DNS is also used to balance traffic globally, so the data for a name may differ in different parts of the internet.

The document then lists the failures most often seen as operator signing errors. The first is a timing problem with the signature records: each signature has an inception time and an expiry time between which it is valid, and letting that time pass without creating a new signature is one of the most common DNSSEC errors. To a lesser extent the same happens if signatures were made active before their inception time. For all of these, the primary check is on the data, and signature expiration is about the only error seen on actual data such as www.example.com. All the other errors relate to the chain of trust established by the delegation records in the parent zone and the key records in the child zones, and mostly occur during key rollovers, though they are not limited to that. The second is that the key records in a child zone do not match the delegation record in the parent zone, which can happen at many points in the key lifecycle; DNSViz is the best tool for showing problems in the chain, and when debugging by hand, dig with the multiline option shows the key identifier of a key record. The variations are a delegation record pointing to a key that does not exist in the child zone, a delegation record pointing to a key that exists but is never used to make signatures, and data that does not match on both sides, which is more common in initial setup when something was copied by hand. The document ends by saying that this is only a starting point, and that it is not possible to provide a simple checklist for deciding whether a domain is broken by an attack or by an operator error.
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting a domain that fails validation, the operator has to work out whether the domain broke itself or somebody broke it. The clues are consistency and history: does the same failure appear on different resolver implementations, from different parts of the world, and on every authoritative server? Does the address the domain resolves to still look right, even though the signatures are wrong? And has the domain changed recently? An expired signature or a mismatch between the parent's record of the child's key and the child's own key are the usual operator mistakes.

sections.title: Security Considerations and Broken Domains
sections.content:
End-to-end DNSSEC validation will be disabled during the time that an anchor is used. The anchor may also still be in place after the time when the misconfiguration that caused validation to break has been fixed, so there may be a gap between the moment a domain has been re-secured and the moment the anchor is removed. An anchor may also be put in place by a resolver operator without the knowledge of the authoritative domain administrator, although attempts should be made to contact and inform the administrator first. One side effect of implementing an anchor is that it may break client applications that assume a domain is signed and expect the Authentic Data bit in the response, though many applications that require DNSSEC perform their own validation, so this should not be a major issue.

The document also compares this with other kinds of DNS misconfiguration. Domain administrators are ultimately responsible for their records, and resolver operators cannot and should not correct misconfigured address, alias, mail exchange or other records of domains for which they are not authoritative. Expecting non-authoritative entities to protect domain administrators from any misconfiguration is unrealistic and unreasonable, and in the long term it is harmful to the delegated design of the DNS. With DNSSEC breakage, however, it is often possible to tell that there is a misconfiguration by looking at the data, without needing to guess what it should have been.

Some domains are broken on purpose, such as dnssec-failed.org, for testing. A user querying a validating recursive resolver for such a domain should fail to resolve and should get a Server Failure error, response code 2, and if such a domain resolves successfully, that is a sign the resolver is not fully validating. An organisation that uses anchors should not add one for an intentionally broken domain, and the requirement to attempt to contact the zone's administrators is what prevents that from happening. An organisation running an intentionally broken domain may wish to add a text record saying that the domain is purposely broken for testing purposes.
sections.plainLanguage: While an anchor is in place, that domain is not checked at all, and it may stay unchecked for a little while after the domain has been fixed. It can also upset applications that expect to be told the domain is signed. The document is clear that a resolver must not start fixing other people's DNS records, and that a domain broken on purpose for testing should fail to resolve rather than be rescued by an anchor.

viz.caption: A POSITIVE TRUST ANCHOR AND A NEGATIVE ONE

cells: Starts the authentication chain for a signed response
Stops the authentication chain being validated
The response is validated and the Authentic Data bit is set
Upstream responses are treated as if the zone were unsigned, and no Authentic Data bit is set
A public key in a DNSKEY record or a hash of one in a DS record
A local setting in the resolver, named differently by each implementation
Takes precedence over a positive trust anchor at the same node, disabling it

viz.caption: THE RULES FOR USING A NEGATIVE TRUST ANCHOR

items.title: Limited duration
items.text: It must only be used for a limited time, with an end time and date set.

items.title: Never automatic
items.text: Use of an anchor must not be automatic; a person decides.

items.title: One branch only
items.text: It applies to a specific domain or sub-domain and to nothing else.

items.title: Nothing up the chain
items.text: Names above it, such as the parent zone and the root, are still validated.

items.title: Nothing else in the tree
items.text: A different branch of the name tree is not affected.

viz.caption: THE CLUES THAT SEPARATE A MISTAKE FROM AN ATTACK

items.title: Other implementations
items.text: Does the failure appear on every vendor's resolver, or only one?

items.title: Everywhere
items.text: Is the same error seen around the world and from all the authoritative servers?

items.title: The data itself
items.text: Has the address the domain resolves to stayed the same? If so, it points to operator error.

items.title: History
items.text: What did the domain look like before? A passive database or DNSViz may hold the answer.
